rule.description: The session connection policy for the shared CURL handle (network socket re-use and permitted transfer protocols) is a single session-level decision with a single input. The rule counts the distinct functions that apply that policy directly to the handle via raw, unchecked curl_easy_setopt calls, and is violated when more than one function does, because a conceptual change to the policy then requires coordinated edits at every applying site instead of one location.

detection: clang-tidy cert-err33-c confined to ::curl_easy_setopt with --system-headers surfaces every raw (result-discarding) curl_easy_setopt call site in the translation unit; the classifier keeps the sites whose option argument encodes the connection policy, attributes each site to its enclosing function, and reports the distinct applying functions.

checks.description: Direct application of the network socket re-use policy attribute at multiple independent handle-lifecycle sites.
checks.detected_relation: enclosing function -> raw unchecked curl_easy_setopt(CURLOPT_FORBID_REUSE) on the shared handle
checks.why_this_is_the_smell: Each of these five functions independently stamps the socket re-use attribute derived from the session policy, so deciding 'does this session hold sockets open' is repeated along the whole handle lifecycle instead of being applied in one location; changing the decision or the attribute requires touching every stamping site.

matches.evidence: http.c:482 stamps CURLOPT_FORBID_REUSE from the shared policy flag during module initialization, on a handle eagerly created at startup.
http.c:1028 stamps CURLOPT_FORBID_REUSE from the shared policy flag in the handle acquisition path that every request passes through.
http.c:1068 stamps CURLOPT_FORBID_REUSE from the shared policy flag after the library-level reset returns the handle to startup defaults.
http.c:1183 stamps CURLOPT_FORBID_REUSE from the shared policy flag inside the option-application branch, before the user-chosen option value is applied.
http.c:1310 stamps CURLOPT_FORBID_REUSE from the shared policy flag in the request runner itself, leaving the cached flag as the per-request policy source.

checks.description: Direct application of the permitted-protocol policy attribute at multiple independent handle-lifecycle sites.
checks.detected_relation: enclosing function -> raw unchecked curl_easy_setopt(CURLOPT_PROTOCOLS_STR / CURLOPT_PROTOCOLS) on the shared handle
checks.why_this_is_the_smell: Which transfer protocols the shared handle may speak is part of the same session connection policy, but it is re-stamped by additional sites in the handle acquisition and reset paths, so the protocol part of the policy lives in yet more places than the re-use part.

matches.evidence: http.c:1031 stamps the permitted-protocol attribute (protocol list string on this libcurl) raw and unchecked in the handle acquisition path.
http.c:1070 stamps the permitted-protocol attribute raw and unchecked immediately after the library-level reset, duplicating the acquisition-path stamp.

excluded.reason: raw unchecked curl_easy_setopt calls for CURLOPT_CONNECTTIMEOUT_MS, CURLOPT_TIMEOUT_MS and CURLOPT_USERAGENT: per-request default values inherited from the clean revision, not session connection policy, so they are not matches of this rule.

the raw unchecked CURLOPT_TCP_KEEPALIVE stamp in the injected fragment re-applies the keepalive opt-in knob (the policy's input), not one of the rule's policy attributes; it is visible to the analyzer but deliberately outside the policy-attribute set.
curl_easy_setopt sites wrapped in the module's error-checked CURL_SETOPT macro consume the return value, so they are not raw applications and are mechanically excluded by the analyzer.
the policy-input predicate derives input state from the settable-option table but applies nothing to the handle; the rule measures where the policy is applied, not where its input is read.
